name: St Bartholomew's Church, Brighton
text: Your train passes near St Bartholomew's Church in Brighton, on the train's {side}, opened in 1874. It has no tower or spire, but its roof rises 135 feet; one of its critics called it "a Noah's Ark in brick".

name: London Road Viaduct
text: Your train passes near the London Road Viaduct, on the train's {side}, which carries the line to Lewes across a valley in Brighton. Built in 1846, it curves sharply on 27 arches and took about ten million bricks.

name: Clayton Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Clayton Tunnel, more than a mile long and finished in 1841, the longest tunnel on the line to Brighton. Its northern entrance is turreted like a castle, with a small cottage perched on top.

name: St John the Evangelist's Church, Burgess Hill
text: Your train passes near St John the Evangelist's Church in Burgess Hill, on the train's {side}, a Gothic Revival church of local brick consecrated in 1863. It was the town's first Church of England church.

name: Burgess Hill
text: Your train passes through Burgess Hill, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. Until the 19th century much of it was St John's Common, grazing land where a Midsummer Fair was held every June 24th.

name: Plumpton Racecourse
text: Your train passes near Plumpton Racecourse, on the train's {side}, where racing began in 1884. The Queen Mother had her first winner here in 1963, and AP McCoy won his 3,000th race here in 2009.

name: Battle of Muster Green
text: Your train passes near Muster Green in Haywards Heath, on the train's {side}, where Parliamentarians beat a larger Royalist army in December 1642. It was the furthest any large Royalist force got into Sussex during the Civil Wars.

name: Ouse Valley Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the Ouse Valley Viaduct, 96 feet high and carried on 37 arches, with stone balustrades along the top. It opened to trains in July 1841, and has been called "probably the most elegant viaduct in Britain".

name: Worth Forest
text: Your train passes near Worth Forest, on the train's {side}, an ancient wood in a ghyll, a narrow valley that a stream has cut into soft sandstone. Its wet valley floor is carpeted with sphagnum moss.

name: Tree House, Crawley
text: Your train passes near Tree House on Crawley's High Street, on the train's {side}, the town's original manor house, built in the early 15th century. It is named after an ancient elm that stood outside for hundreds of years, and is now home to Crawley Museum.

name: The George Hotel, Crawley
text: Your train passes near the George in Crawley, on the train's {side}, once the most important coaching inn in Sussex, halfway between London and Brighton. Its inn sign, which reaches across the High Street, began as a gallows.

name: Ifield Water Mill
text: Your train passes near Ifield Water Mill, on the train's {side}, a weatherboarded 19th-century mill on the site of an earlier iron forge. It fell out of use in the 1930s; volunteers later restored it to working order.

name: Roffey Road Halt
text: Your train passes the site of Roffey Road Halt, opened in 1907 for steam railmotors in the hope that houses would be built nearby. They weren't, and it closed in 1937; a few concrete posts from its platforms are all that remain.

name: Horsham Museum
text: Your train passes near Horsham Museum, on the train's {side}, founded in 1893 by volunteers from the town's Free Christian Church. It has been in Causeway House, a building listed Grade II*, since 1941.

name: Chesworth House
text: Your train passes near Chesworth House, on the train's {side}, a Tudor manor house of the Dukes of Norfolk. Catherine Howard spent her childhood here before she married Henry VIII, who had stayed here himself in 1519.

name: Christ's Hospital
text: Your train passes near Christ's Hospital, on the train's {side}, a school founded in London in 1552 as a charity for poor children. Its pupils still wear a Tudor uniform of long blue coats and yellow socks, worn since 1553.

name: Old Swan Bridge, Pulborough
text: Your train passes near the Old Swan Bridge over the River Arun at Pulborough, on the train's {side}, built in 1787 in a medieval style. It replaced a line of timber bridges, and before them a ferry.

name: St Botolph's Church, Hardham
text: Your train passes near St Botolph's Church at Hardham, on the train's {side}, whose 12th-century wall paintings are the earliest nearly complete series in England. Among them is the earliest known picture of St George in the country.

name: Amberley Museum
text: Your train passes near Amberley Museum, on the train's {side}, an open-air museum of industry in an old chalk quarry. The quarry had its own railway, linked to the main line at Amberley station; the museum runs passenger trains on a narrow-gauge line today.

name: College of Richard Collyer
text: Your train passes near the College of Richard Collyer, on the train's {side}, founded in the will of Richard Collyer, a Horsham man who became a wealthy London mercer, in 1532. The Mercers' Company are still its trustees.

name: Shiremark Mill, Capel
text: Your train passes the site of Shiremark Mill, on the train's {side}, a windmill built in 1774 just inside Surrey, close to the border with Sussex. It worked by wind until 1919, and burnt down in 1972.

name: Ockley station
text: Ockley station, at one end of this stretch, opened as Ockley & Capel in 1867. Next to brickworks, it carried bricks for many years, and milk until the 1930s; it is listed Grade II.

name: Church of St Mary, Pixham
text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary at Pixham, on the train's {side}, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens in 1903. Inside, it has a barrel-vaulted ceiling.

name: Denbies Wine Estate
text: Your train passes near Denbies Wine Estate, on the train's {side}, the largest vineyard in England, with more than a tenth of all the vines planted in the United Kingdom. It takes its name from John Denby, who owned the farmhouse here in the 16th century.

name: The Running Horse, Leatherhead
text: Your train passes near the Running Horse in Leatherhead, on the train's {side}, a pub by the River Mole dating back to 1403. It was first known as Rummings House, after Eleynor Rumminge, the subject of a poem by John Skelton, Henry VIII's poet; the poem is on a wall inside.

name: Thorndike Theatre
text: Your train passes near the Leatherhead Theatre, on the train's {side}, built inside a disused 1930s cinema and opened by Princess Margaret in 1969 as the Thorndike Theatre. It was named after the actor Dame Sybil Thorndike.

name: Bookham Commons
text: Your train passes near Bookham Commons, on the train's {side}, woods and grassland owned by the National Trust and mentioned in the Domesday Book. A group of houses on the commons is called the Isle of Wight.

name: The Forest and the Highlands
text: Your train passes near the Forest and the Highlands, on the train's {side}, a wood owned by East Horsley's parish council where almost 180 kinds of plant and more than 50 kinds of bird have been recorded, among them tawny owls and nuthatches.

name: West Horsley Place
text: Your train passes near West Horsley Place, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house of the 15th century with 50 rooms. It is best known as the filming location of the BBC series Ghosts.

name: Abbot's Hospital
text: Your train passes near Abbot's Hospital on Guildford's High Street, on the train's {side}, founded in 1619 by George Abbot, Archbishop of Canterbury, as homes for the town's elderly. Its first residents moved in on his 60th birthday in 1622.

name: Royal Grammar School, Guildford
text: Your train passes near the Royal Grammar School in Guildford, on the train's {side}, founded in the will of Robert Beckingham, who died in 1509. Its Old Building, put up between 1557 and 1586, holds a rare chained library.

name: Cobham Training Centre
text: Your train passes near Chelsea Football Club's training ground, on the train's {side}. The first team have trained here at Stoke d'Abernon since 2005.

name: St Mary's Church, Stoke d'Abernon
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Stoke d'Abernon, on the train's {side}, parts of which date from the 7th century. In front of the altar rail is the brass of Sir John d'Abernon, who died in 1277, one of the finest in existence.

name: Oxshott Heath and Woods
text: Your train passes near Oxshott Heath, on the train's {side}, common land of woods and heath on a sandy hill. From its top, which has a war memorial, you can see as far as Box Hill.

name: Scilly Isles, Surrey
text: Your train passes near the Scilly Isles, on the train's {side}: not the islands, but a double roundabout built in the 1930s. Drivers called its unfamiliar traffic islands the "silly islands", and the name stuck.

name: Surbiton Studios
text: Your train passes near the site of Surbiton Studios, on the train's {side}, a film studio opened in 1918 whose first film came out in January 1919. It belonged to Stoll Pictures, one of the largest British film companies of the early 1920s.

name: Seething Wells
text: Your train passes near Seething Wells, on the train's {side}, where the Lambeth Waterworks opened in 1852 to take cleaner water from the Thames above the tide. It played a part in John Snow's study of cholera in London.

name: Wayneflete Tower
text: Your train passes near Wayneflete Tower, on the train's {side}, the gatehouse of a palace built at Esher in 1462 by William Waynflete, Bishop of Winchester. Most of the palace was pulled down in the 17th century, but the tower survives, listed Grade I.

name: Ashley Park, Surrey
text: Your train passes near Ashley Park, on the train's {side}, where a grand country house stood from 1605 until the early 1920s. Its owners included the Duke of Dorset and members of the Sassoon family; its grounds are now streets of detached houses.

name: Oatlands Palace
text: Your train passes near Oatlands, on the train's {side}, where Henry VIII acquired a manor house in 1538 and rebuilt it as a palace for Anne of Cleves. Much of its foundation stone came from Chertsey Abbey; little of the palace remains.
